pl-l4d31c7-d1e112.summary: Explains that the evil of incontinence is that a man knows his wife beyond the need of procreating children, but the good of marriage is also there: marriage with intercourse beyond the intention of generation is not therefore not good; the good is not made culpable by that evil, but the evil becomes venial because of the nuptial good, and the Apostle reproves the evil of incontinence, not marriage.
claims: The nuptial good makes the evil of incontinence venial.

pl-l4d31c7-d1e121.summary: Quotes Augustine: marriage does not compel intercourse not for offspring but obtains its pardon, provided it is not so excessive as to impede times due to prayer, nor turned to unnatural use. Intercourse necessary for generation is blameless and alone nuptial; that which exceeds need follows lust, not reason, and to render it, not demand it, belongs to the spouse, lest the other fornicate; if both are subject to such concupiscence, they do what is not of marriage, of which marriage is not the instigator but the intercessor. Conjugal honor is chastity and the faith of procreating and rendering the debt, which the Apostle defends from all sin.
claims: Marriage obtains pardon for intercourse beyond need.
Rendering the debt is part of marriage; demanding beyond need is not.

pl-l4d31c7-d1e138.summary: Continues: since intercourse with the intention of generation, properly attributed to marriage, is not culpable, the Apostle grants by pardon only that spouses demand the debt from desire for pleasure, not offspring; this pleasure does not become culpable because of marriage, but receives pardon because of it; so marriage is praiseworthy, making pardonable even what does not belong to it.
claims: Marriage makes pardonable what exceeds its purpose.

pl-l4d31c7-d1e145.summary: Concludes that marriage is wholly good in its kind, since it keeps conjugal faith, unites the sexes for receiving offspring, and abhors the impiety of separation.
claims: Marriage is good in its kind.

pl-l4d31c7-d1e152.summary: Adds that an unbelieving spouse cannot harm the holiness of marriage; rather the believing spouse benefits the unbeliever, as the Apostle teaches.
claims: An unbelieving spouse does not harm the marriage's holiness.

pl-l4d31c7-d1e158.summary: Concludes that the holiness of marriage and the nuptial good defend from sin spouses who unite only for offspring or who render the debt when asked; if conjugal intercourse could not be without sin, God would not have commanded after the flood 'increase and multiply', when they could no longer unite without carnal concupiscence.
claims: Intercourse for offspring or rendering the debt is without sin.

pl-l4d31c7.summary: The evil of incontinence, knowing one's wife beyond the need of procreation, coexists with the good of marriage, which is not made culpable by it; rather that evil becomes venial because of the nuptial good. Augustine: marriage does not compel such intercourse but obtains pardon for it, provided it is not so excessive as to impede times of prayer nor turned to unnatural use; rendering the debt to prevent the spouse's fornication belongs to marriage, demanding beyond need is fault; marriage is not the instigator but the intercessor of that fault. So marriage is good in its kind, keeping faith, joining for offspring, and abhorring separation; even an unbelieving spouse cannot harm its holiness. Those who unite for offspring or render the debt are defended from sin, else God would not have commanded procreation after the flood.
claims: The evil of incontinence becomes venial through the good of marriage.
Rendering the debt is part of marriage; demanding it beyond need is venial fault.
Unnatural use of marriage is not excused.
Marriage is good in its kind.
Intercourse for offspring or rendering the debt is without sin.
